content.title: Antiderivatives and Substitution
content.overview: Integration by substitution, often called u-substitution, is the reverse process of the chain rule. It is used to evaluate integrals of composite functions by transforming the variable of integration to simplify the integrand.
learning_objectives: Identify a composite function and its inner derivative within an integrand.
Perform a change of variables using u-substitution for indefinite and definite integrals.
Transform the limits of integration for definite integrals when using substitution.
Justify the validity of an antiderivative using the reverse chain rule.

sections.title: The Spot-and-Substitute Strategy
sections.content:
The primary trigger for u-substitution is an integrand of the form f(g(x)) multiplied by g'(x), or a constant multiple of g'(x). The goal is to simplify the integral into a basic form, such as the power rule or a transcendental function. The process involves three main steps: 1. Identify the 'inner' function g(x) and set u = g(x). 2. Calculate the differential du = g'(x) dx and solve for dx or substitute the entire g'(x) dx term. 3. Rewrite the entire integral in terms of u, ensuring no x terms remain.

![A linear flow chart showing the steps of u-substitution: Identify u and du, Convert limits, Rewrite integral in u, Integrate and evaluate.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/4c9a7653-dc4e-4a61-8e66-8486cf113376-1786519372469-565.webp)

sections.title: Definite Integrals and Changing Bounds
sections.content: When applying substitution to a definite integral, you must account for the limits of integration. Because the limits a and b are x-values, they must be converted to u-values using the substitution formula u = g(x). If the original integral is from x = a to x = b, the new integral is from u = g(a) to u = g(b). Once the bounds are changed, you evaluate the antiderivative at the new u-limits directly; there is no need to 'back-substitute' the original x-expression.

sections.title: Justification via the Reverse Chain Rule
sections.content: The validity of u-substitution rests on the Chain Rule. If F is an antiderivative of f, then the derivative of F(g(x)) is F'(g(x)) * g'(x) = f(g(x)) * g'(x). Therefore, the integral of f(g(x)) * g'(x) dx is F(g(x)) + C. To verify any result, differentiate your final antiderivative; it must return the original integrand.

worked_examples.question: Evaluate the definite integral I = ∫ from 1 to 4 of [2x / (x² + 1)] dx exactly.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the inner function. Let g(x) = x² + 1. Its derivative g'(x) = 2x is present in the numerator. Step 2: Set u = x² + 1. Then du = 2x dx. Step 3: Change the limits of integration. When x = 1, u = (1)² + 1 = 2. When x = 4, u = (4)² + 1 = 17. Step 4: Rewrite the integral: I = ∫ from 2 to 17 of (1/u) du. Step 5: Integrate. The antiderivative of 1/u is ln|u|. Step 6: Evaluate at the new bounds: ln(17) - ln(2). Using log properties, the final exact value is ln(17/2).

common_mistakes: Forgetting to calculate du and simply replacing dx with du without adjusting for g'(x).
Failing to change the limits of integration in a definite integral, leading to evaluation at the original x-values.
Leaving 'x' variables in the integrand after substituting 'u', which creates an invalid mixed-variable expression.
Neglecting the constant of integration (+C) for indefinite integrals.
exam_tips: If the derivative of your chosen 'u' is missing a constant, you can multiply and divide by that constant to complete the substitution.
Always check for continuity of the integrand on the interval [a, b] before applying the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
On free-response questions, clearly state your substitution (e.g., 'Let u = ...') and show the transformed limits to earn full justification points.
content.recap: U-substitution reverses the chain rule by identifying an inner function u = g(x) such that its derivative g'(x) is a factor in the integrand. For definite integrals, limits must be updated to u-values, allowing for direct evaluation without returning to the original variable.

knowledge_claims.content: U-substitution is triggered when an integrand contains a composite function f(g(x)) and the derivative of the inner function g'(x) as a factor.
The first step in u-substitution is defining u as the inner function g(x) and calculating the differential du = g'(x) dx.
When performing u-substitution, every instance of the original variable x and the differential dx must be replaced by terms involving u and du.
For definite integrals, the lower limit a and upper limit b must be converted to g(a) and g(b) respectively.
If the limits of a definite integral are correctly changed to u-values, the integral can be evaluated using the antiderivative in terms of u without back-substituting the original x-expression.
U-substitution is the integration equivalent of the chain rule for differentiation.
To verify an indefinite integral result obtained by substitution, differentiate the result to see if it matches the original integrand.
A common error is treating du as equivalent to dx without accounting for the derivative of the inner function.
If the derivative of the inner function differs from the integrand's factor by only a constant, u-substitution is still applicable by adjusting the constant.
The differential du represents the rate of change of u with respect to x multiplied by the change in x (dx).
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus requires the integrand to be continuous on the interval of integration for the substitution method to be valid for definite integrals.
Unlike indefinite integrals which require back-substitution to the original variable x, definite integrals with transformed bounds are evaluated directly in u.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Antiderivatives and Substitution — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Antiderivatives and Substitution: Antiderivatives reverse differentiation, and substitution recognizes a composite integrand paired with an inner derivative.
options.B: Exponential Growth and Decay: When a rate of change is proportional to the current amount, the solution is exponential and its constant is determined by contextual data.
options.C: Second Derivatives of Parametric Curves: A parametric second derivative differentiates dy/dx with respect to the parameter and divides by dx/dt again.
options.D: Integral and p-Series Tests: Positive decreasing terms may be compared with an improper integral, and a p-series converges exactly when its exponent exceeds one.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because Antiderivatives reverse differentiation, and substitution recognizes a composite integrand paired with an inner derivative. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Antiderivatives and Substitution — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Logistic Differential Equations: Logistic growth includes a carrying capacity, has maximum growth at half that capacity, and approaches equilibrium rather than increasing without bound.
options.B: Antiderivatives and Substitution: Antiderivatives reverse differentiation, and substitution recognizes a composite integrand paired with an inner derivative.
options.C: Vector-Valued Motion: Differentiating a position vector gives velocity, speed is the magnitude of velocity, and acceleration is the velocity derivative.
options.D: Comparison and Limit Comparison Tests: Positive-term series can inherit convergence or divergence from a benchmark through inequalities or a finite positive ratio limit.
